set.overview: Donaldson, at 4,140 feet, has no maintained trail. Walkers reach it by taking the unmarked Seward herd path to the ridge and following the crest toward Emmons, with the summit sitting a few steps to the left of the track. It is a rugged day on eroded, steep ground where map and compass skills matter more than the modest Class 2 rating suggests.
set.approach: Park in the lot at the end of the gravel stretch of Corey's Road, outside Tupper Lake. Follow the red-marked Blueberry Trail, not the wetter horse track beside it, for roughly 4.7 miles: it passes the Calkins Brook path junction near 1.2 miles, crosses a big brook around 3.5 miles, and goes by the Blueberry lean-to near 4.5 miles. Turn right onto the Ward Brook Truck Trail, cross the next brook, and look for the cairn that starts the Seward herd path.
set.descent_text: From the summit area, step back along the ridge path for about a fifth of a mile, then turn left onto the unmarked Calkins Brook herd path. It runs about 2.5 miles with steep pitches and stream crossings before meeting the marked trail, which leads back to the parking lot. Walking out the way you came in is the alternative.
hazards: No official trail on the peak: map and compass navigation is needed on the herd paths
The ridge is very muddy in places and has blowdown across the path
Steep, eroded ground on the Seward approach, with rocky sections that can ice over in winter

review.notes: Only source read describes the Seward-Donaldson-Emmons loop (15.8 mi, 4,050 ft), which includes other peaks, so gain and distance skipped. Season not stated on any page read. Descent text describes the Calkins Brook loop-out; the page itself is a loop so a pure retrace is also offered.

set.approach: Start from the parking lot at the end of the gravel part of Corey's Road. Take the Blueberry Trail about 4.5 miles over flat to rolling ground, then turn right onto the Ward Brook Truck Trail, an old woods road. Walk past the Ward Brook lean-to and watch for the cairn marking the Seymour herd path, which follows a brook before turning steeply uphill.
set.descent_text: Retrace the herd path to the Ward Brook Truck Trail, then follow it and the Blueberry Trail back to the parking lot. The upper path is steep and often greasy, so descend slowly and place feet carefully.
hazards: Steep herd path with footing that is often very slippery, worst on the way down
Several junctions, bridges and unmarked sections to keep track of
Upper slope needs snow spikes or crampons when icy in winter

evidence.fact: 14 miles round trip out and back, so 7 miles one way = 11.27 km

review.notes: Distance halved from the stated out-and-back. Second source not opened. Season skipped, none stated.

set.overview: Sawteeth is a 4,100-foot High Peak on the Adirondack Mountain Reserve, climbed as an out-and-back by way of the Weld Trail. The day is mostly a long road and lakeside walk followed by a climb to the Pyramid and Gothics junction and a short, steep, eroded pitch to the top that includes a rock slab.
set.approach: Park at the St. Huberts lot on Route 73 outside Keene Valley, where a reservation is needed from May 1 to October 31. Walk the dirt road to the paved road by the golf course, turn left at about half a mile to reach the reserve gate, then follow Lake Road roughly 3 miles to Lower Ausable Lake and cross the bridge below the dam. Pass the Scenic Trail junction and the Rainbow Falls side path, then climb 1.6 miles to the Pyramid and Gothics junction.
set.descent_text: Come down the same way: drop the steep, eroded half mile to the Pyramid and Gothics junction, then follow the Weld Trail back past Lower Ausable Lake and walk Lake Road to the St. Huberts lot.
hazards: Final half mile is steep and eroded, with a rock slab to cross
Long road and bridge sections and several junctions make the way out easy to misjudge when tired
Upper slopes can need snow spikes or crampons in winter

evidence.fact: 12 miles round trip via Weld Trail out-and-back, so 6 miles one way = 9.66 km

review.notes: Distance halved from the stated round trip; single source. Hiking Project page covers only the 0.5 mile summit spur. Season skipped: only a parking-reservation window was stated, not a climbing window.

set.overview: A roughly 2,000-foot rock slide on Cascade Mountain visible from the highway. A blocky lower section leads to a waterfall over 100 feet tall that is climbed on fourth-class holds, then a few third-class steps give way to a gentler middle. The top is a steep slabby headwall that is easy fifth class if climbed, or avoidable by scrambling left, followed by glades and a thick spruce bushwhack to the summit.
set.approach: Park at the Cascade Lakes day-use area on Route 73, where the slide can be seen from the road. A short path of under five minutes leads from the lot to the foot of the slide, and the climbing starts right away on the blocky lower section below the waterfall.
hazards: Loose rock on the waterfall section
Exposure on the fourth-class waterfall and the headwall, where a fall would be serious
Steep slab headwall at the top that some parties rope up for

review.notes: Descent and season not covered on either page, skipped.

set.overview: A twelve-pitch trad line up the north face of Fairview Dome, graded 5.9 and among the most popular long routes in the Tuolumne area. It follows a continuous crack and slab system up the broad granite face, and the walk-in is short enough to make it a full day on the wall.
set.approach: Park at the obvious roadside pullout on the south side of the road, roughly 3.5 miles from the Tuolumne store and 4 miles from Tenaya Lake. A walk of about 15 minutes along the base leads to a point near the center of the dome, where the route starts.
set.descent_text: Walk off the dome by heading south down easy low-angle slabs to the ground, then follow the base of the dome back to your packs and the trail. Allow about half an hour to 45 minutes.

review.notes: Overview is thin on character because the page had little beyond grade and pitch count; the 'continuous crack and slab system' phrase should be checked or trimmed. Season and hazards skipped: only a peregrine closure window (Mar 1 to Jul 15) was stated, which is access, not a hazard or season.

set.overview: A big, imposing wall above the lake, first climbed in the early 1960s: thirteen pitches of alpine trad, about 1,500 feet, rated 5.8+. The rock is steep and smooth with squared, angular holds linking broken cracks rather than granite. The line starts up a left-hand gully, traverses right, climbs the face and a shallow dihedral, then finishes through a notch and along the summit ridge.
set.descent_text: Cross class 3 rock toward the Ken-Clyde notch, then downclimb the couloir to the start of the route. At least one rappel is needed, and parties descending the summit ridge may use two or three depending on rope length. Snow or ice in the couloir changes how it goes.
hazards: More loose rock than is usual on the route
Route-finding is hard where several lines overlap
Snow and steep ice in the descent couloir, with snow on the approach early in the season

review.notes: The 'description' fill is written to the overview column because the brief allows only overview; overview here already holds old text, so this overview replaces it keeping its facts (first climbed early 1960s, squared holds). Gain and distance skipped: only a user comment gave about 8 miles from a different trailhead. Descent rappel count varied (1 to 3), stated loosely.

set.approach: Start at the Onion Valley trailhead and climb about 5 miles and 2,600 feet to Kearsarge Pass. Drop roughly 1,400 feet over about 3 miles to Charlotte Lake, then continue about 3.5 miles to the base of the south face, a total near 13 miles. Bear canisters are required on the approach trails.
set.descent_text: After the summit, walk off the dome and return the way you came: back to Charlotte Lake, up to Kearsarge Pass, then about 4 miles downhill to the Onion Valley parking lot. The trip out is roughly 12.5 miles.

review.notes: Page distances contradict each other (13 mi in vs 12.5 out; 9.5 mi/3,500 ft vs 8.5 mi/2,100 ft). Gain/distance skipped as crag-style and inconsistent. Hazards and season not stated for this route; skipped. The descent text calls the way off a walk-off, which the page labels 'walkoff' without describing the terrain.

set.approach: Follow the approach trail up and left to the smaller wall below the main ledge, known as Tombstone Ledge. The route starts there on a serrated crack system just right of the sport line Boot Hill. Some parties begin on the second pitch around the corner from Corrugation Corner, though skipping the first pitch is not recommended.
hazards: Ankle-breaking ledge just below the pitch-one crux
Pitch two offwidth is the route's crux and has a hard reputation
Exposed arete and ledge on pitch three with only two fixed pins

review.notes: A 2026 raptor closure warning exists on the page; not added as a hazard. Season skipped, none stated. The walk-off path destination ('back down to the base') is my inference of where the ridge trail goes; trim if unwanted.

hazards: Rockfall from the cliffs on either side of the couloir
The couloir steepens to 45 to 50 degrees near the top, and a fall from high up can slide a long way
Avalanche terrain: snow conditions decide where the snow climbing begins

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: the page gives only 3.5 miles and about 1,840 ft to Grizzly Lake, not the summit. Season not stated (only a spring photo caption).

set.overview: The east ridge is the standard Class 2 way up Stewart Peak, a remote 13,988-foot summit in the San Juans. The day is a faint creek trail, a climb through trees to the ridge crest near 12,300 feet, and a long grassy and talus ridge walk with a rugged section near 13,100 feet that is bypassed on the left.
set.approach: Drive the long, rough dirt road from Gunnison to the Nutras Creek trailhead at about 11,000 feet, a small lot with room for a handful of cars. Follow the faint trail southwest up Nutras Creek for about 2.5 miles, crossing a side creek near 2 miles. Around 11,800 feet, leave the creek and head northwest through the trees to reach the east ridge near 12,300 feet.
set.descent_text: Go back down the ridge the same way, aiming to be below treeline before afternoon storms build. Pick up the faint Nutras Creek trail again carefully, since it is easy to lose on the way out.
hazards: Faint, hard-to-follow creek trail makes route-finding the main challenge
Moderate rockfall potential on the rocky ridge sections
Exposed above treeline from about 12,300 feet with no shelter from afternoon storms
Snow can linger on the ridge into early summer

evidence.fact: about 3,000 ft gain, 8.25 miles round trip from Nutras Creek
East Ridge listed as 8 miles, 3000 ft gain, trailhead and one-way status not stated
8.25 miles round trip, so 4.125 miles one way = 6.64 km

review.notes: Worklist row says mileage depends on the Stewart Creek road; the East Ridge figures here are from the Nutras Creek trailhead, which is a different start (a southwest ridge route from Stewart Creek is 15.8 mi RT and was not used). The CMC figure matches but does not name its trailhead, so the numbers stay single-source. Season is from the CMC page only (July through September).
